The surah lets you hear your own endings approaching not as loss but as the call that came to the most beloved of creation ﷺ, and it fills the remaining time with the three verbs that make any ending safe: glorify, praise, seek forgiveness. He is ever-returning to the one who returns.

passages.why: The verse of the harvest: help and opening arriving together after twenty years of refusal.
The manner of finishing everything: praise and pardon at the summit, the verse he ﷺ lived in his final bowings.

connections.why: Al-Kafirun refused the bargain of the idolaters; An-Nasr shows those same people entering the religion in crowds, refusal ripened into welcome.
Al-Fath promised the clear opening; An-Nasr stands on the far side of that promise, watching it fulfilled.

virtue.text: After this surah came down, Aishah relates, the Prophet ﷺ filled his bowing and prostration with, Glory to You, O Allah, our Lord, and praise; O Allah, forgive me, interpreting the Quran in his own limbs, so the surah carries a sound portrait of how he ﷺ received it.

context: Al-Masad descends from a scene preserved in Bukhari. When the command came to warn his nearest kin, the Prophet ﷺ climbed the hill of Safa and called Quraysh clan by clan. If I told you horsemen were in the valley behind me about to attack, would you believe me? Yes, they said, we have never known you to lie. Then I warn you, he ﷺ said, of a severe punishment ahead. His own uncle Abu Lahab answered: tabban laka, ruin to you, is this what you gathered us for? And the surah came down carrying his word back to him: tabbat yada Abi Lahab, ruined are the hands of Abu Lahab.

Abu Lahab, Abd al-Uzza ibn Abd al-Muttalib, and his wife Umm Jamil, sister of Abu Sufyan, made a household of the persecution: he dogged the Prophet’s ﷺ steps crying liar, and she, the carrier of firewood, fed the fires of slander, or laid thorned branches in his path as some early commentators relate. The surah then became a standing wager the Quran placed on its own truth: it declared, while both lived, that they would die outside faith and burn. Either could have falsified the Book with one spoken shahadah, testimony of faith. Neither ever did. Abu Lahab died soon after Badr, untouched by belief, and the prophecy closed.
surahs.name_story: The surah is named for al-masad, the rope of twisted palm-fiber around the neck of the firewood-carrier in its last verse. It is equally known as Surat Tabbat from its first word and Surat al-Lahab from the man it condemns, whose nickname, father of flame, was given for his glowing face and answered by the Flame it names.

movements.note: The ruin he pronounced falls back on his own hands; his wealth and all he earned avail him nothing, and a fire of lahab, of flame, waits to match his name.
His wife, hauler of wood for slander’s fires, enters the scene with a rope of twisted fiber on her neck, the couple’s shared cruelty given one shared sentence.

themes.d: The condemned man is the Prophet’s ﷺ own uncle: nearness of blood to the best of creation saves no one who chooses enmity to his message.
Revealed while both targets lived free to fake a conversion and shatter it, the surah wagered the Quran’s truth on two human hearts and won.
Ma aghna anhu maluhu wa ma kasab: neither fortune nor achievements ransom a soul, the refrain of this whole final section of the mushaf.
The father of flame ends in flame: the surah turns his proud nickname into his sentence, and mockery of the truth into a mirror.

heart: Al-Masad is the only surah that condemns a contemporary of the Prophet ﷺ by name, and reciting it slowly one feels why it was preserved for all time: it is the Quran’s demonstration that no rank, no lineage, no wealth, and no proximity to holiness substitutes for faith. Abu Lahab had every advantage a soul could hold, Hashimi blood, wealth, the Prophet ﷺ as his own nephew, and the surah shows all of it weightless against one hardened heart. The reciter quietly checks his own borrowed credentials, family piety, community, reputation, and lets the surah strip him back to the only question that counts: what does my own heart hold?

There is also a strange comfort here for anyone opposed by their own kin for their faith. The Prophet ﷺ himself was cursed by his uncle and slandered by his uncle’s wife, and heaven answered on his behalf. The surah teaches the wounded believer to leave the answering to Allah, whose replies outlast every insult.

passages.why: Hear a curse reversed in real time: the ruin he pronounced on Safa returned to his own hands.
One verse retires the oldest false hope: wealth and earnings availing nothing at the reckoning.
The final image, the fiber rope, where the surah’s justice reaches even the carrier of the firewood.

connections.why: Al-Kawthar reverses a taunt against the Prophet ﷺ, Al-Masad reverses a curse: two enemies handed the endings they designed for him.
Al-Humazah draws the type, the mocker rich enough to sneer; Al-Masad names the case and closes the file.

virtue.text: No hadith assigns a recitation reward to Al-Masad, and it needs no certificate: its distinction is to be a fulfilled prophecy, revealed in Bukhari’s sound account at Safa and verified by two lives that never falsified it.

context: Al-Ikhlas came down as an answer. The transmitted reports, graded fair by many scholars, relate that questioners demanded of the Prophet ﷺ, unsub lana rabbaka, trace your Lord’s lineage for us, idolaters of Makkah in one report, and in another, questioners in Madinah, which is why the scholars differ over its Makkan or Madinan origin. The surah replied with a definition that refuses all lineage: He is Allah, Ahad, uniquely One; as-Samad, the self-sufficient on whom all depend; He neither begets nor is begotten, and none is equal to Him.

No surah saturated the Prophet’s ﷺ daily worship more. He paired it with Al-Kafirun in the sunnah of Fajr and the rak’ahs after tawaf, sealed his witr with it, and recited the three Quls over his palms each night. When a commander of an expedition ended every recitation with it and was asked why, he said: because it is the description of ar-Rahman, the Most Merciful, and I love to recite it. Tell him, said the Prophet ﷺ, that Allah loves him.
surahs.name_story: Al-Ikhlas means pure sincerity, and the surah never uses the word: it earned the name by being purely about Allah, no command, no story, no other subject, and by purifying the creed of whoever holds it. It is also cited as Qul huwa Allahu Ahad from its opening, and some early books call it Surat at-Tawhid, the surah of divine oneness.

movements.note: The identity is stated in two names: Ahad, One without division or series, and as-Samad, the eternal refuge whom all creation needs and who needs nothing.
The negations that guard the affirmation: no offspring and no origin, and none in all existence is kufuwan, equal or comparable, to Him.

themes.d: Ahad is not the first of a series but the One who admits no series: unique in essence, names, and deeds, beyond division and beyond counting.
Every creature leans on Him for every breath while He leans on nothing: the name that turns all human dependency into an address.
Lam yalid wa lam yulad: the surah fences the truth against every mythology of divine families, and against every subtle modern idol.
The Quran teaches creed, law, and the accounts of nations; this surah carries the creed whole, which is how the scholars explained its equivalence to a third.

heart: Al-Ikhlas recited slowly is the heart returning to its one fixed point. Four verses, and every direction of human worship is corrected at once: Ahad dissolves the crowded pantheons, ancient and modern, and as-Samad quietly redirects all our leaning, on salaries, on people, on our own competence, toward the only support that does not itself need supporting. The reciter feels the surah working like a plumb line dropped through the self, truing whatever had tilted toward created things during the day.

Its shortness is its mercy and its test. Said in seconds, it can pass unweighed; said with presence, it is the heaviest speech a tongue can carry, the description of ar-Rahman by ar-Rahman. The Companion who could not stop reciting it was told that Allah loved him, and that door is not closed: love of this surah is love of the One it describes, and He answers it in kind.

passages.why: The Quran’s definition of God in His own words: hear Ahad and let it empty every false throne.
As-Samad: the name to lean on when every created support has bent.
The final fence: none is equal to Him, the verse that completes the creed in seven words.

connections.why: Al-Kafirun and Al-Ikhlas travel together in the Prophet’s ﷺ prayer: the first is disavowal of every false god, the second the description of the true One.
Al-Falaq begins the two refuges that follow: after the creed is pure, the believer is taught to shelter it.

virtue.text: The Prophet ﷺ said that Qul huwa Allahu Ahad equals a third of the Quran, a sound and famous virtue, and he ﷺ told the man who loved it because it describes ar-Rahman: Allah loves him.
virtue.src: Bukhari 5013, Muslim 811; the love report, Bukhari 7375

context: Al-Falaq came down paired with An-Nas, and the Prophet ﷺ announced them with wonder: do you not see verses revealed this night the like of which has never been seen? Qul a’udhu bi-rabbil-falaq and Qul a’udhu bi-rabbin-nas. The account is in Muslim from Uqbah ibn Amir. The scholars differ whether the pair is Makkan or Madinan; many tafsirs connect them to the sound Bukhari account of the spell cast on the Prophet ﷺ by Labid ibn al-A’sam, though the link of their revelation to that event is a later addition, and honesty keeps the two reports distinct.

What is beyond dispute is how he ﷺ used them. Aishah relates that every night he would cup his palms, recite Al-Ikhlas, Al-Falaq, and An-Nas into them, and wipe over his body, and in his final illness she did it for him with his own hands. He taught them as the morning and evening shield, and said that nothing compares to them for the one seeking refuge. With these surahs the community learned that fear has a liturgy: darkness, sorcery, and envy are real, and the answer to all three is a Lord who splits the dark with dawn.
surahs.name_story: The surah is named for al-falaq, the daybreak, the splitting-open: the Lord who cracks the night with dawn, the seed with the shoot, and every siege with rescue. With An-Nas it forms al-mu’awwidhatan, the two surahs of seeking refuge, a title given by the Prophet ﷺ himself.

movements.h: Refuge with the Splitter of dawn
movements.note: The command is to say it aloud: I take refuge with the Lord of the daybreak from the evil of what He created, all harm at once placed under the authority of its own Maker.
Then the fears are named one by one and shrunk by naming: the settling night, the blowers on knots practicing sorcery, and the envier when he envies.

themes.d: Isti’adhah, taking refuge, is said, not merely felt: qul, say it, the soul physically running to its Lord the way a child runs behind a father.
From the evil of what He created: harm has no independent throne; it exists inside His dominion, which is exactly why refuge with Him works.
Night, sorcery, envy: the surah drags the vague dreads of the heart into the light and lists them, and a named fear is already half-disarmed.
Idha hasad, when he envies: the eye’s harm activates when envy acts, so the surah teaches both refuge from enviers and vigilance against becoming one.

heart: Al-Falaq recited slowly is the believer’s answer to the dark, and its first word of address is already the cure: not Lord of the night, but Lord of the daybreak. The surah makes you seek shelter from darkness with the One whose signature is splitting it, so hope is built into the grammar before any fear is named. Then the three darknesses file past, the night that hides things, the malice that works unseen, the envy that smiles to your face, and the reciter realizes the surah has covered every direction harm arrives from: circumstance, enemy craft, and the resentful heart nearby.

Whoever makes this surah a nightly habit, palms cupped as the Prophet ﷺ taught, discovers its quiet psychological gift: fear is no longer managed alone. The dark is still dark, but it has an owner, and you know Him, and the last thing your body feels before sleep is His name wiped over it.

passages.why: The address that carries the cure: refuge from darkness sought with the Lord of the daybreak.
The last named fear, envy, the harm that arrives through a smiling face, placed under His protection.

connections.why: An-Nas is its inseparable twin: Al-Falaq shelters from harms outside the chest, An-Nas from the whisper inside it.
Al-Ikhlas states the creed and the two refuges guard it: the Prophet ﷺ recited the three together each night over his palms.

virtue.text: The Prophet ﷺ said of Al-Falaq and An-Nas: verses revealed this night the like of which has never been seen, and he made them his nightly and morning refuge, reciting them over his palms and wiping his body.

context: An-Nas closes the Quran, revealed together with Al-Falaq as the two refuges the Prophet ﷺ said were without like. Where its twin lists harms of the outer world, night, sorcery, envy, this surah turns entirely inward to a single enemy, the last one standing when all others fall: al-waswas al-khannas, the whispering one who retreats, murmuring into the chests of mankind, whether that whisperer is of the jinn, the unseen beings of smokeless fire, or of people, for harmful suggestion can arrive in a friendly human voice.

There is a quiet architecture in the Quran ending here. The Book opens with Al-Fatihah, mankind asking guidance from the Lord of the worlds; it closes with mankind running to the Lord, King, and God of mankind to protect that guidance from the voice that would unpick it. The Prophet ﷺ sealed his nights with this surah among the three Quls, and taught that the whisperer shrinks and retreats, khannas, the moment Allah is remembered, so the surah is not only a prayer but a tactic.
surahs.name_story: The surah is named for an-nas, mankind, sounded five times in six verses like a bell: named for the ones it protects rather than the enemy it exposes. With Al-Falaq it forms al-mu’awwidhatan, the two refuges, the Prophet’s ﷺ own name for the pair that ends the Book.

movements.note: Refuge is sought in an ascending claim: Rabb, the Lord who nurtures mankind, Malik, the King who rules them, Ilah, the God they worship, care, then authority, then devotion.
The threat is exposed with precision: the retreating whisperer who murmurs in the chests of mankind, whether from the hidden jinn or from people.

themes.d: Lord, King, God: three relationships, each one enough, stacked into a single refuge, because the enemy attacks the deepest room in the house, the chest.
Khannas, the shrinking one: his entire power is suggestion, and he flees the name of Allah, so the surah carries its own victory condition inside it.
Min al-jinnati wan-nas: harmful whispering is not only unseen; it can come dressed as advice from people, and the surah teaches discernment about voices.
The Book’s last word of substance is mankind sheltered in its Lord: revelation ends by tucking the reader under the wing it opened.

heart: An-Nas recited slowly is the most intimate security the Quran offers, because it guards the one territory no lock defends: the interior murmur. Every believer knows the voice, the suggestion that arrives mid-prayer, the doubt seeded at night, the resentment dressed as reason, and the surah’s mercy is to tell you two things about it: it is real, you are not uniquely broken, and it is weak, built to retreat the instant your Lord is named. Reciting the surah is therefore not describing the battle but winning the day’s round of it.

And the three titles are the deep comfort. Against a whisper you are given a Lord who raised you, a King who outranks every power that threatens you, and a God worth all your worship, three ropes for one small enemy. The Quran ends here deliberately: after every law, story, and warning, the final gift is a hiding place. The reader closes the Book already inside it.

passages.why: The beginning of the Quran’s last prayer: refuge sought with the Lord of mankind for mankind.
The enemy named exactly: the whisperer who retreats, so the reciter learns his weakness in his name.

connections.why: Al-Falaq guards the outside of the fortress and An-Nas the inside: the Prophet ﷺ recited the pair as one shield.
Al-Fatihah opens the Book asking guidance, An-Nas closes it guarding that guidance: the Quran begins in prayer and ends in refuge.

virtue.text: With Al-Falaq it forms the two refuges the Prophet ﷺ called verses without like, revealed in one night; he recited them in the nightly three over his palms and after every prayer, and no seeker of protection was ever given their equal.
